court: New York Supreme Court, General Term
holding_summary: The habendum clause limiting use of a leased camp-meeting cottage lot to 'a private residence' did not by itself bar the lessee from keeping boarders and lodgers for hire there. However, a by-law of the lessor association forbidding the keeping of boarders and lodgers for hire without its consent was a valid limitation binding on the lessee under the lease's incorporation of the association's constitution and by-laws. The court therefore affirmed an injunction restraining the defendant from keeping boarders or lodgers for hire on the premises.

quotes.text: We think, therefore, there is nothing in the habendum clause which should be held to restrain the defendant from doing what he is shown to have done, by way of keeping boarders and lodgers for hire, at his residence.

the by-laws, rules and regulations of the association forbid the keeping of boarders and lodgers for hire, on the grounds of the association by any person whomsoever, without the special consent of the corporation.
the defendant in keeping boarders and lodgers for hire is violating a by-law enacted by the lessor which was binding upon the lessees and which the plaintiff has the right to enforce against him.

holding_summary: The court held that letting furnished apartments to lodgers by the month did not breach a lease covenant against under-letting or assigning, because an apartment occupant holds only a license-like right to occupy designated rooms rather than an estate carved out of the term. The lessor's acceptance of rent for a series of years with knowledge that the building was operated as an apartment house was construed as a license to use it that way, not a mere recurring waiver. The lessee therefore did not forfeit the lease by letting apartments to monthly lodgers.

quotes.text: Letting rooms to lodgers is held not to be a breach of a covenant against under-letting. Doe v. Laming, 4 Camp., 73. See, also, Wilson v. Martin, 1 Den., 602; White v. Maynard, 111 Mass., 250.
The interest of an occupier of an apartment is peculiar. He has simply the right to occupy designated rooms during tho time specified, but a destruction of the building ends the right

the conduct of the defendant in receiving for a series of years without objection, the rent due on the lease, with knowledge of the actual situation, should, if necessary, be construed as a license to use and occupy the building as an apartment house, and not as a mere waiver from time to time of a particular antecedent breach of the covenant.
